INTRODUCTION

Wershikwir, or Werchikwir,! is the name given by Khowar-speakers to the
dialect of Burushaski speken by the indigenous inhabitants of Yasin These
latter people call themselves Buriisho, and their language Burushaski, just ng the
people of Hunza do,

Kho. Wersh- no doubt represents Bur. Buriish-; Kho. -ik denotes “ people
{of)”’, ag in Yasinik, “ people of Yasin”; and Kho. -2dr denotes “ Innguage
specch (of)"’, as in Khowar, “ the language of the Kho.” Khowar-speakers alsc
use the word Wershigim a3 an equivalent fur Yasin.

In the Census of 1931 the population of Yasin was recorded as 8,084, of whom
7,518 were Werelulwar-spenkers. These included 2,506 who were bilingual
speaking both Werchikwar and Khowar.

The use of Khowar in Yasin is no doubt accounted for by the fact that before
the British-Indian Government took over charge of the Gilgit region, towards
the end of the nineteenth century, Yasin had long been controlled by members
of the aristocratic Khushwaqt family of Chitral, who were Khowdr-speakers,*
Subsequently under the British régime the various persiuus appointed as Governors
of Yasin were all, I believe, of Chitrali stock. Khowar has therefore for long been
the official language in Yasin.

The Werchikwar Vocabulary here presented is based mainly on a collection
of words which I obtained by word of mouth from Muslim, son of Bal, of Naxbar,
Yasin. I had known and worked with Muslim in 1923-4, and L renewed acquaint-
ance with lim when I paid a visit to Yasin in April, 1935.5 I secured his services
again and he came and stayed with me in Aliabad in HMunza from the middle of
May to the middle of July, 1935.

The words I got from him I wrote down on separate slips, evidenUly very
hastily. There are over 3,000 of these slips. I have now not the slightest recollection
how the words came to be chosen. Muslim (‘ M.") also dictated Texts Nos. 1-V
to me. He also supplied lists of numerals, paradigms of some verbs, and other
miscellancous information about houses, cattle, mills, ete,

Muslim was bilingual, speaking both Werehikwar and Khowir. In 1923-4
he had supplied me with Khowar texts, and it was only in 1935, when F secured
his services again, that I learned that his actual mother-tongue was Werchikwar.
He had also a working knowledge of Hindustani.

The author of this work, Lt. Col. D. L. BR. Lorimer, died on 26th February,
1962, at the age of 85 years. Ina letter to this Institute dated 18th February, 1957,
he wrote: “It may mildly interest you to know that I have this year been doing
some work on preparing 8 Vocabulary of Werchikwar, with a few Texts. At my
present rate of progress, which will certainly not be increased, it will not be
finished, Jet alone revised and typed in my lifetime.”

He was able, however, to inform us on 9th May, 1960, that he had finished the
work, and in November of the same year he accepted our offer of publishing it.
In spite of failing eyesight and declining physical forces, he was able during the year
1961 to do the proof-reading and supervise the printing.

We deeply regret that he did not live to see the book out of press and to receive
our thanks for his helpful co-operation in bringing out this publication, which sheds
light on a hitherto little known language.

Another source of information wis a series of Werchikwar words recorded
on slips in Arabic and Roman scrij". with explanations chiefly in Hindustani,
but with meanings sometimes in English. ‘These were supplied to me in 1935 by
Mihtarjau Shahzada Ytsuf of Siime!. ° 5.Y." was an educated aristocrat, being,
I think, a member of the Khushwayt family of Chitrali origin referred to ahove.
le was also an old friend, who had finished me with Khowar material in 1923-4,
and had also enabled me to obtiin the Werchikwar Texta published in The
Burushaski Language, vol, ii. His own language was Khowar, and though he
understood fairly well, I believe, !oth Werchikwar and Burushaski, and had a
Werchikwar-speaking retainer, his |mowledge of the grammar, and of the
differences between Hunza Burushas!i and Werchikwar appears not to be very
precise. The slips of Werchikwar words supplicd by him number about 1,900.
Of these words some four-fifths arc in the sroup with initials from a- to j-. Ido
not remember, but I think that I mut hive given hin the typescript, or proofs
then beginning to come in, of the Hurushaski Vocabulary in The Burushaski
Language to work from. It looks as if a gacd many of his words and grammatical
forms may have been derived from th \t source. For instance he gives, apparently
as the Infinitive of Werchikwar verte, the Hunza Bur. Infin. form, eg. elas, “ to
do,” which in Werch. has only the Noun Agent meaning “doer”, a meaning
which it can also have in Bur. It is also to be remembered that when he made
up this list of words he was living wilh me in Aliabad, in a Hz.Bur. environment,
which might at any time have influenced both him and his retainer,

In view of all this I have exercised considerable discretion in utilizing 8.¥.’s
material, omitting words and forms which seem probably to have come from
Hunza Burushaski sources. There remain, however, a good many words, special
meanings, and phrases, which seem to deserve inclusion as being at any rate
known to Werchikwar-speakers, All such I have distinguished by the initials
8.Y.

I am greatly indebted to Shahzada Yusuf for the hard work he put into
preparing this list of words. I ought to add that both in 1923-4 and 1934-5 I also
obtained Khowar material from 8.Y., and in a good many cases where a
Werchikwar word here is compared to a Khowar word, information about tho
latter may, in whole or in part, have come from 8.Y. I should like to say here
how grateful I am to him for all that he did for me in years now long past.

Earlier at Aliabad in November, 1934, before I had recovered Muslim, 8.¥.
had also supplied Texts Noa. VI and VII. Seeing how incorrect they were gram-
matically, T lefé them aside and did not seek to get any more from this source.
T now reproduce them, however, because they probably represent a low-grade,

but real, type of Werchikwar speech. Werchikwar is stigmatized by the Burusho
of Hunza and Nagar as a very corrupt form of Burushaski (V. Vocab., s.v., yé"-),

x Werchikwar-Fnglish Vocabulary

and in 1946, when Lieut. R. 0. Carter was travelling in Yasin, Werchikwar
incurred the contempt of his Hunza servant. It remains for some future inquirer
to study Werchikwar as it is actually spoken in daily life by various grades of
speaker in Yasin. He could also determine whether the form ‘ Werchikwar ”
is permissible, or ought to be banned.

I have mule no attempt here to deal with the grammar of Werchikwar. The
notes on Werchikwar given by me in The Burushaski Language, vol. i, pp. 422-452,
taken in conjunction with the full Grammar of Hunza Bur. will be sufficient,
I think, to meet the essential needs of anyone using the Vocabulary and Texts
here presented. I have, however, provided a statement of the principal forms of
the Numerals and paradigms of the verbs ba-, “to be"; tser-, “to go”; and
tsucr-, “ to come,” obtained from Muslim. These are more complete than those
given by mein the Bur. Lang., vol. i, or by Zarubin. Zarubin’s remains, of course,
the fullest exposition of Werchikwar Grammar, For some of us it suffers from
the handicap of being written in Russian. In 1927, knowing no Russian, I worked
through it word by word with a dictionary. Fortunately I noted down the
meanings of most of the words.

Like all pioneer work, such as Zarubin’s or my own, it is open to criticism
on particular points. For instance, at the bottom of page 285, Zarubin gives the
“ Demonstrative Pronouns” as follows :—

I. Category Sg. ne PI. we refers to men (or, males ? D.L.)
II. Category ,, mu ,, we ,,  ,, Women (females ? D.L.)
Ilf. Category ,, se ,, ce ,,  ,, animals
IV. Category ,, fe ,, ke ,, ,, inanimate objects.

Introduction xi

se and ce, my x. forms se and tse, also, of course, refer to many inanimate
objects, as well as to animals (other than human) of cither sex.

Tam far from making any claim to infallibility for myself, especially where
Werchikwar is concerned !

Once again I have to express my gratitude to the Leverhulme Research Awards
Committee for the generous financial aid which enabled me to revisit Gilgit in
1934-5, when I collected the material on which this book is based.

D. L. R. L.
4th May, 1960.

The woman having made thin flaps of dough and having cut them into strips —
by the time she has made ready, water is boiling—bringing the strips of dough she
puts them in the water. When they have cooked and become ready, she takes them
out. Pouring them into a dish, she leaves it there till it cools, When it has cooled,
she serves it up (lit. down). She sets it before the (inembers of the) family, (and)

before the guest.

Bringing raw milk to the boil, they proceed to make curds. When it (the milk)
has set, it becomes “ triy ”. When they pour it out, it becomes “ qurut”. Bringing
milk to the boil, they pour it on the “ gurut ”. That day they extract curds (mai)
from the “ gurut” (or, the g. becomes curds 2). The next day they take up the
“qurut”, After that (?) the milk coagulates, With a spoon they beat the curds
(mai) from the “ qurut”. Having done so and having brought water to the boil—it
is realy here—they put two or three spoonsfuls of cold milk with the “ mai”
(curds). They pour milk on the “ mai” which was in the dish (note, “i.e. only
two spoons or so of ‘ mai’ to three or four seers of milk”). Putting on the lid
they put a quilt over it, so that the air (“ wind”) may not play on it,

Still more material having come to light, I can now add the following comments
on some of the words given above under the heading “ Seasons ,
fadary 38 the Kho. equivalent of the following entry, Werch. bo-yiy irsa. They
denote the period 2]st February to 25st March, the Zodiacal month of Tfiit.
Thisis the time of sowing, following the “ Taking out of the Seed " by the Tham.
ayga'yo. This does refer to the putting up of thorn fences, ete., to protect the
coming crops. It is carried out in the month of Boyiy Hesa and is followed by

Bur. datimu etas and Kho. dagfi korik are given by 8.Y. as one of the affairs of the

With x. plural subjects there seems to be some latitude in regard to the
inflectional endings of the Future and Preterite tenses.
In the Fut. there are the alternative endings :—
-imi and -emen (this latter the bh. 3rd. pl. ending).
In the Pret. there are the alternatives :-—

-imi and -ex (the latter the h. 3rd. pl. ending).
Examples: Fut. (in the paradigms) Aayura éser‘emi, “ the horses will go ” ;
hayura ts'u-rcmen, “ the horses will come.”
dolants ts.hu‘rimi, “ avalanches will come (down).” ILL. 29,
Pret. huka tenjo fucten, “the dogs ate the bones.” IIT. 44.

little other material the two forms in the Fut, are in about equal use, while in the
Pret. the -en predominates, but this may be accidental.

yeyum, the Pres, Pe. form of *-yan-, “to take.” In Wercht. this form also acts as
a Verbal Noun, where in Hz. Bur. the Infinitive form (here *-y.10.18) would be
used. yayum, “ taking ” here seems to denote “ taking out", “carrying out”.
In Khowar the same ceremony is called bi xezik, “ to take out, or, the taking

out of, the seed,” and I recorded an account of itn Yasini Khowarin 1923-4.

(1) lrba’s, this probably only refers to the ordinary dressing up by women at
festival times. There is no further mention of dress, unless official gifts of
clothing and cloth are reckoned as falling under this head.

bo yeryum barn, in Hz. Bur. the Pres. Tense can have the meaning “to be going
to (do s.t.)”.

savatan, for this originally guntsan, “a day,” was recorder.

Thame ta, here grammatically ia must refer to sart-ita, but semantically one
would expect it to relate to ataleya, as in the similar passage in Text 2.2.
Perhaps the speaker inserted the words bo . . . du‘lum ka on a last moment
impulse.

bande'$ cé1mi, note the consistent use throughout this text of the Fut. (Pres.)
Tense in place of the Pres. Tense, which would be used in Hz. Bur. and is used
in T.2, 4-7.

(2) gungat, was here glossed : “ from 6 to Tam.”

isover, for shikar.” The word is used with reference to small game, here probably
for hawking, or possibly shooting, birds. The Dat. Suffix -ar is the Fz, form.

yalawar eryaréiman, glossed: “ this is at the Yasin ¢ha'y, in the morning,

10-11 a.m., when the Tham has returned.” The thay is described as the Tham’s
bakery which appears to be more or less open to the public. Tt seems to he
used of the publie part of the Tham’s residence, and of his residonee in general.

(3) 'e'sqar'akimen, this is annotated: “ they put up marks of flour, with wooden
stencil,” followed by the expressions: yar'ei kun'a. ha (yore't?) Eapat.
'esqarakinas kun'a, Tam extremely doubtful about the use or even existence
of atencils in Yasin. More probably what is denoted is some kind of “ st ick”
(kuna), or “ trowel”, “ spatula” (fap.f).

At this point there is an enigmatic note: “‘selrn (= silarcin) female
(sc. relation 2). Don’t come in from other houses.” This probably means
that outside, unrelated, women are not allowed to come into the tha-y.

Bar'rs, Bare’s, also recorded in Kho, as Bar'e's. It was described as: Berriéue
Dehtsum yate, ie. “ above the Berichu Village”, or, “‘ the Doms’ Village,”
and as: Maniéi Bore hiltse se doy bt, i.e. it is the elevated place at the
edge, or mouth (2) of the Manichi atream, or nullah ”. Manich, Manich Gol,
and Damandeh, representing the above placcs, are shown in the Survey of
India ¢ inch to the mile map No. J. 43, T., published by W.O., 1942, about
a couple of miles south of Yasin Fort.

I have also a Yasini Khowar text, recorded in 1923-4, which describes
the same custom under the title of “ Bar'es Nisi-k”, i.e. “ The going out to
Bares”. In it Bares is described as a “ level (or, smooth) place above (or,
on the top of ?) Bujaiyot, at the lower end of Yasin”. (Yasino poyga Bujai-
yorto teka Ladt Zay'a.)

Notes

This text did not start as a planned text. Muslim, my informant, was telling
me something of his family history, and after some brief notes 1 began to write
down what he sail. This, like Text No. 3, was finally dated 15.7.35. Additional

No. 1. About the “ Taking out of the Sced ”

(1) The Seed rejoicing, and the Seed dress, and the Seed ceremonial are o
this wise: firatly the Tham saying (to himself) “ They are going to take out th

we take out the seed?” On his saying this, the officials and elders fix a (a
auspicious) time. When they have done so, the Tham gives instructions to th
Atalegh in accordance with what has been his practice and procedure.

(2) In the evening they take the seed. Getting up early in the morning th
Tham goes off to Sandi for hunting. Having gone for hunting, making all th
servants who are (with him) and the people of Sandi make up bundles of thor
bushes and bring them along, he returns (to the Yasin Fort), Then they fetch th
Bandsmen, and the Bandsmen coming to the Fort play the “ gh'alawar” (i«
the polo tune).

No. 2, The Bares Show

(1) In olden times the Bares show used to be (carried out) in this way : there
was a watchman on the look out, he was on the road. In spring when they took
out the seed and cultivation had begun, the Tham used to go out to Bares to look
(at the land). Going up on to Bares and looking up (the valley) he used to view
the (cultivated) land of Yasin. Having done so, he would ask, Why have they
left so many of these fields fallow ?”

(2) On his saying this, very superior elders and officials would reply, “ Sir,
(the owner of onc} is a watchman (who is} on duty. Another is a poor man and has
no (plough) oxen. Another is an orphan who has no seed-grain. (So these fields)
have remained (uncultivated), On their saying this, the Tham would give orders
to his officials : “ Plough (his) land for the watchman who is on duty. (As rewards)
the orphan who has no seed, give him seed out of my revenne (grain). To the man
who has no ox give plough-oxen.” After issuing orders he used to return (to
the village).

No. 6. The Old Woman and her Nephew

(1) In former times an old woman had a nephew (or, grandson). The old
woman had four male friends. The nephew was antipathetic to the old woman.
Every day the old woman used to go to a shrine (and say), “ My nephew is repug-
nant to me,” Her nephew inquired of her, “ O old woman (or, Granny), why do
you go to the shrine?” “Task for long life for you,” replied the old woman.
The nephew said, “ O old woman (or, Granny), a holy man bas died at a certain
place. That place is famous. If anyone forms some desire and goes there, that
desire of his will be granted,”

(2) On (hearing) this statement she started out, and the nephew set ont
secretly after her. Arriving at the place before the old woman, he seated himself
unseen in the cell {of the shrine). The old woman arriving there, said, ‘‘O Holy

No. 7. The She-Goat and the Bear

(1) There was a she-goat, The goat had three kids. Shutting up the kids,
she used to go off to feed. After feeding she used to come back and call out to
them, “ Let me in.” On her saying this, the kids used to let her in, Going in she
used to suckle the kids. Every day she used to do thus. One day a bear came and
ate up the kids. Afterwards the goat coming back called out (to them), No sound
came from inside. Opening the door the goat went in. The kids weren't there.

(2) She then went to lodge a complaint with the king. The king gave the goat
an iron svord, and he gave a wooden sword to the bear, Then the goat and the
bear fought. The goat smote the bear with the sword and killed it. The kids
came out of the bear's belly. After that the goat took the kids and went away.
